source.title: Introspective X Training: Feedback Conditioning Improves Scaling Across all LLM Training Stages
source.authors: Brandon Cui; Ximing Lu; Jaehun Jung; Syeda Nahida Akter; Hyunwoo Kim; Yu-Xiao Qu; David Acuna; Shrimai Prabhumoye; Ye-Jin Choi; Prithviraj Ammanabrolu

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present. Some table formatting is flattened, but the scaling-curve outcomes relevant here are described in text.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps training compute and measures downstream benchmark scores, a different measure from held-out cross-entropy loss and parameter/token scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper reports downstream benchmark performance against compute for fixed-size models, but does not report held-out cross-entropy scaling, fitted power laws, extrapolation from small runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Other benchmark comparisons at single training budgets and cited scaling-law results are not rows for the tested scaling version.
record.test_reason: A method paper (Introspective Training, IXT). Its 'scaling curves' are downstream benchmark scores against total FLOPs for one fixed-size 7.5B model under continued training, plotted only to compare IXT with the NTP baseline. It fits no power law, reports no held-out loss, varies no model size, and does not assess whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss. It uses Kaplan's 6N/2N FLOP approximation as a tool. Every recorded row is the study's own method compared with a baseline, so none bears on V6 or any other version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that feedback conditioning (IXT) 'bends scaling curves', giving up to 2.8x FLOP efficiency over NTP. They also report that it surpasses NTP asymptotes on fixed corpora, persists at 12T/18T checkpoints and in SFT, and spills over to general benchmarks with 15% of data annotated. 'Scaling curve' here means downstream score versus compute for fixed-size models. They make no claim about loss power laws, extrapolation or compute-optimal allocation.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains models with feedback-conditioned documents and reports downstream benchmark scores against compute, rather than measuring held-out cross-entropy scaling across parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported gains vary by benchmark domain and data setup: math and coding show compute-efficiency gains, while general benchmarks are similar early and show a smaller advantage later. The paper also reports feedback-format and inference-prefix effects, but these are not tests of the scaling-law versions recorded here.

fits_no_version.finding: On a fixed corpus (Swallow Code, Mbase 7.5B), the NTP HumanEval curve plateaus with more epochs and compute. The authors describe this as an 'asymptotic performance limit' that IXT surpasses. No values or fit are given.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream accuracy under repeated continued pretraining on a fixed domain corpus saturates, and the ceiling depends on the training objective or conditioning.

fits_no_version.finding: In Appendix F, training on only the top-quality tier of Crane Math degrades MATH and GSM8K past roughly 1e21 FLOPs, while larger mixed-quality subsets keep improving monotonically (Figure 9, downstream only).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream returns to compute under heavy data repetition turn negative when the unique-data pool is small.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported for the relevant scaling-curve results. The evidence is downstream benchmark performance from compute sweeps on a fixed-size model; it does not establish predictive power-law fits, held-out loss scaling, or scaling across model sizes.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit. Single-budget downstream comparisons were not entered because they do not test performance predictability with scale or compute.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no scaling in parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs extrapolated to larger runs.
No depth, width or shape comparisons at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes. Repeated-data epochs appear only as downstream curves with no loss law.
Downstream scores are plotted against FLOPs for a single model size, but there is no assessment of predictability from scale or from pretraining loss, and no fit.
No fitted exponents and no fitting-choice analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' with a V6 'supports' label should be dropped. The rows are IXT-vs-NTP gaps, which are method comparisons, and V6 is about whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or loss; this paper never assesses that. The FLOP curves vary only training duration on one model size and report no values or fits.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining-loss measurements or scaling against parameter count, training tokens, or compute under non-bottleneck conditions.
No fits from small runs or predictions evaluated on substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute optimization over parameter and token allocations.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No tests of the claimed loss law across other modalities or the listed training regimes.

The study measures downstream benchmark performance against training compute in selected sweeps, but does not fit a predictive relation to scale or pretraining loss, and does not test predictability across model sizes.
The paper does not analyze fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits, or test how those depend on parameter counting, schedules, data, or fitting method.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested downstream benchmark compute sweeps on the 7.5B Mbase model
reader_labels.reason: Across the reported sweeps, downstream scores improve relative to NTP at matched compute, with compute-efficiency gains in math and coding; the general group is similar at 0.25 epochs and ahead by +1.5 at 1 epoch (r1–r6).
